title: Ovarian Cancer - Persistent Bloating and Abdominal Distension
patient_instructions: You are Margaret Wilson, a 58-year-old retired teacher. For the last 8-10 weeks you have felt increasingly bloated and your abdomen looks swollen - you have had to loosen your waistband. You feel full very quickly when eating (you can only manage small meals) and have a vague dull lower abdominal discomfort. You have also been needing to pass urine more often and more urgently. Your appetite is down and you have lost a few kilograms without trying. Your bowels are a little more constipated than usual. You went through menopause at 51 and have had NO vaginal bleeding since. If asked: no fevers, no vomiting, no severe pain. Family history (only if asked directly): your mother had breast cancer in her 60s; you are not aware of any ovarian cancer. You have never had genetic testing. You have two grown children, never used the pill for long. Your ideas: you think it is 'just my age' or maybe irritable bowel or trapped wind. Your concerns: privately you are frightened it could be something serious because it is not going away. Your expectation: you want to know what is causing it. You are anxious but composed. If told it may be serious, ask 'Do you think it could be cancer, doctor?'
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Margaret Wilson, 58, presents with several weeks of progressive bloating and abdominal distension. In 8 minutes: take a focused history, explain your leading diagnosis and differential to the patient, and outline your initial investigation and referral plan. The examiner will tell you that abdominal examination reveals distension with a fixed lower abdominal mass and shifting dullness consistent with ascites. Communicate your findings and plan to the patient.
examiner_instructions: This tests recognition of ovarian cancer as a serious not-to-be-missed cause of persistent bloating/early satiety/urinary urgency in a woman over 50. If asked, provide: abdominal distension, a firm irregular pelvic/lower abdominal mass, and shifting dullness (ascites). Reward a candidate who arranges transvaginal/transabdominal ultrasound and serum CA-125 (with CEA and CA19-9 to help exclude a GI primary), references the Risk of Malignancy Index, and makes an URGENT referral to a gynaecological oncologist / specialist multidisciplinary team (not routine gynaecology). Reward asking about a family history of both breast AND ovarian cancer and considering BRCA/Lynch. The candidate should explain CA-125 supports but does not confirm the diagnosis (raised in benign conditions) and that definitive diagnosis is surgical/histological. Prompt if needed: 'What single tumour marker and which specialist team?'

criteria: Elicits the ovarian cancer symptom cluster (persistent bloating, early satiety, abdominal/pelvic pain, urinary urgency/frequency) and duration >few weeks in a woman >50
Screens weight loss, altered bowel habit and post-menopausal bleeding
Takes a family history of breast AND ovarian cancer and considers hereditary risk (BRCA/Lynch)
States suspected ovarian malignancy as the leading diagnosis given the mass and ascites
Gives a sensible differential (bowel cancer, IBS, ascites of other cause, fibroids/endometriosis)
Explains CA-125 supports but does not confirm; definitive diagnosis is surgical/histological
Arranges transvaginal/transabdominal ultrasound plus serum CA-125 (and CEA/CA19-9 to help distinguish GI primary)
References Risk of Malignancy Index and makes URGENT referral to gynaecological oncologist/MDT (not routine gynaecology)
Explains a serious provisional diagnosis honestly and sensitively without premature certainty
Responds to the patient's fear and checks understanding

red_flags: Persistent bloating, early satiety, abdominal distension and urinary urgency for more than a few weeks in a woman over 50 - suspect ovarian cancer
Palpable fixed/irregular pelvic-abdominal mass with ascites (shifting dullness)
Unintentional weight loss with new altered bowel habit
Any post-menopausal vaginal bleeding (separate red flag for endometrial pathology)
australian_guidelines: Cancer Australia clinical practice guidance for the investigation of symptoms of ovarian cancer: women over 50 with persistent abdominal/pelvic symptoms warrant prompt investigation with pelvic ultrasound and serum CA-125
RANZCOG/RACGP: a suspected adnexal malignancy (complex/septated mass with ascites) requires urgent referral to a gynaecological oncologist / specialist multidisciplinary team, not routine gynaecology

Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI = ultrasound score x menopausal status x CA-125) is used to triage adnexal masses for gynae-oncology referral; consider CEA and CA19-9 to help exclude a gastrointestinal primary
Consider referral to familial cancer genetics for BRCA1/BRCA2 and Lynch syndrome assessment where family history suggests hereditary risk
learning_objectives: Recognise the non-specific symptom cluster of ovarian cancer as a not-to-be-missed diagnosis in women over 50
Select appropriate first-line investigations (pelvic ultrasound, CA-125 with CEA/CA19-9) and apply the Risk of Malignancy Index
Refer urgently to a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team rather than routine gynaecology
Communicate a serious provisional diagnosis honestly while avoiding premature certainty before histology
key_points: Bloating + early satiety + urinary urgency for weeks in a woman >50 is ovarian cancer until proven otherwise ('silent killer')
Investigations: transvaginal/transabdominal ultrasound and serum CA-125 (plus CEA and CA19-9 to help distinguish a GI primary)
CA-125 can be raised in benign conditions (endometriosis, fibroids, ascites) - it supports but does not confirm the diagnosis
Refer urgently to a gynaecological oncologist/MDT; definitive diagnosis and staging are surgical/histological
Ask about breast AND ovarian cancer in relatives and consider BRCA/Lynch genetics referral

citations.claim: Ovarian cancer is a serious disorder not to be missed and red/yellow-flag reasoning must be applied to non-specific abdominal symptoms in older women rather than dismissing bloating/constipation.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.30

citations.claim: A suspected gynaecological/breast malignancy requires urgent specialist surgical referral on suspicion, supporting the gynae-oncology referral pathway.
